results.title: Field experiment - Wikipedia
results.content: # Field experiment. While naturally occurring experiments rely on an external force (e.g. a government, nonprofit, etc.) controlling the randomization treatment assignment and implementation, field experiments require researchers to retain control over randomization and implementation. In a field experiment, researchers randomly assign subjects (or other sampling units) to either treatment or control groups to test claims of causal relationships. After designing the field experiment and gathering the data, researchers can use statistical inference tests to determine the size and strength of the intervention's effect on the subjects. There are limitations of and arguments against using field experiments in place of other research designs (e.g. lab experiments, survey experiments, observational studies, etc.). These problems can lead to imprecise data analysis; however, researchers who use field experiments can use statistical methods in calculating useful information even when these difficulties occur. Modern use field experiments has roots in the 1700s, when James Lind utilized a controlled field experiment to identify a treatment for scurvy.

results.title: Unit 8: Experimental Research Designs Overview Study Guide
results.content: * A true experiment is a research design that aims to establish cause-and-effect relationships between variables. * Single-factor designs involve manipulating only one independent variable to observe its effects on a dependent variable. * A true experiment involves the manipulation of an independent variable, allowing researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships. * Between-subjects design involves random assignment to different conditions, controlling for individual differences. * Within-subjects design allows each participant to serve as their own control, receiving all conditions to reduce variability. * One-group pretest-posttest design does not control for extraneous variables, leading to potential confounding effects. How do single-factor designs facilitate the examination of the effects of an independent variable on a dependent variable? What strategies can researchers employ to control for order and sequence effects in within-subjects designs, and how do these strategies enhance the validity of the study? A true experiment is characterized by the manipulation of an independent variable, control of extraneous variables, random assignment of participants, measurement of a dependent variable, and replication of the study. Within-subjects designs require fewer participants and are more sensitive to detecting differences due to reduced individual variability, but they may suffer from order and carryover effects. In contrast, between-subjects designs avoid these order effects and are simpler to implement, yet they require more participants and can be affected by greater individual variability, potentially obscuring results. Single-factor designs allow researchers to manipulate only one independent variable while controlling for extraneous variables, enabling a focused examination of its effects on the dependent variable. Researchers can use counterbalancing and block randomization to control for order and sequence effects in within-subjects designs. These strategies enhance validity by ensuring that the order of conditions does not systematically influence results, thereby isolating the effects of the independent variable more effectively. A researcher might prefer a between-subjects design when the potential for order effects is high or when the independent variable has lasting effects that could influence subsequent conditions. results.title: Experiment sample size and run time | LaunchDarkly | Documentation
results.content: # Experiment sample size and run time. This topic explains how to determine the number of contexts to include in an experiment and how long to run the experiment for. The number of contexts you include in an experiment is called the sample size. The larger the sample size for an experiment, the more confident you can be in its outcome. How big your sample size should be and how long you run an experiment for depends on how confident you want to be in the outcome. ## Sample sizes for frequentist experiments. Before you start a frequentist experiment, you can use LaunchDarkly’s sample size calculator to estimate the minimum detectable effect and sample size and duration for your experiments. To learn more about how to calculate sample sizes, read Sample size calculations for frequentist experiments. ## Sample sizes for Bayesian experiments. You can also run experiments for a shorter amount of time if enough contexts have encountered your experiment to determine a winning variation. After you begin running an experiment, the experiment’s **Results** tab displays a sample size estimator in the “Summary” section that gives an estimate of how much more traffic needs to encounter your experiment before reaching your chosen probability to be best or desired significance level. Experiments with more than two variations do not display a sample size estimator. In this example, for a probability to be best of 90%, 2,424 more contexts should be in the experiment before you stop the iteration and roll out the winning variation to all contexts:. To be confident that the winning variation is the best out of the variations tested, wait until the sample size estimator indicates you have reached the needed number of contexts. You can use the exposures graph to understand how many unique contexts have encountered each variation within the experiment over time:. * The table only counts contexts with the same context kind as the experiment’s randomization unit. For example, if your experiment’s randomization unit is `user`, then the table counts only `user` contexts. * If the same context is in the experiment multiple times, the table counts the context only once.
